todays_goal: Learn before testing: use explicit instruction, worked examples, guided practice, and complete written responses.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.previous_learning: Tuesday diagnostic showed some fraction and decimal skills but several Grade 6 topics had not been taught. Wednesday begins the teach-first model.
lessons.course_context: Fraction operations are the opening Grade 6 number-operations work before decimals, ratios, rates, and percent.
learning_objectives: Multiply fractions and mixed numbers.
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions.
Divide fractions using the reciprocal of the divisor.
Show steps and simplify answers.
lessons.why_it_matters: Fraction operations appear in measurement, rates, scaling, science, and later algebraic reasoning.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction whose numerator is at least as large as its denominator.
A fraction made by switching numerator and denominator.
The number or fraction you are dividing by.

lessons.written_instruction: Teach multiplication first: convert mixed numbers, multiply numerators and denominators, simplify. For division, identify the divisor, keep the first fraction, change division to multiplication, and use the reciprocal of the divisor only. Use at least three worked examples before independent practice.

worked_examples.title: Multiply proper fractions
worked_examples.explanation: Multiply numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator; 12/35 is already simplified.

worked_examples.title: Divide fractions
worked_examples.explanation: 1/6 is the divisor, so use its reciprocal 6/1: 2/3 x 6 = 4.

guided_practice.hint: Multiply top by top and bottom by bottom.

exit_ticket.rubric: Converts both mixed numbers and multiplies correctly.
Converts mixed number, uses reciprocal, simplifies.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach first. Work two to three complete examples before asking Atticus to solve independently. Ask which fraction is the divisor during division. If he confuses the reciprocal, reteach with a simpler example rather than giving the answer.
lessons.teacher_notes: Completed work showed fraction multiplication stronger than the Day 1 diagnostic suggested, while fraction division remained inconsistent and required Thursday reteach.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: Theme, significance, and evidence: The Last Pass
lessons.previous_learning: Tuesday showed solid story comprehension but weaker vocabulary-in-context precision, theme statements, and significance explanations.
lessons.course_context: The opening unit builds complete evidence-based reading responses before longer texts.
learning_objectives: Use context to define a word.
State a theme as a complete sentence.
Explain why a detail matters.
Write an objective summary.
lessons.why_it_matters: These skills support analysis in literature, science, history, and research.

vocabulary.definition: Looking around deliberately to gather information before acting.
Why a detail matters or what it reveals.
A brief account of the important events or ideas without opinion.

lessons.written_instruction: Read The Last Pass carefully. Answer every part. For significance questions, explain what the detail proves or reveals. For theme, write a complete message that could apply beyond the story.

worked_examples.title: Theme
worked_examples.problem: A player improves after learning to notice teammates instead of focusing only on himself.
worked_examples.solution: A strong theme could be: People improve when they pay attention to the larger situation instead of only their own actions.
worked_examples.explanation: The statement is transferable beyond one character.

worked_examples.title: Significance
worked_examples.problem: A final pass is described as easy.
worked_examples.solution: Its simplicity shows growth because the player now sees the right option early instead of forcing a difficult play.
worked_examples.explanation: The answer explains what the detail reveals.

guided_practice.prompt: Define scanning from context in the story.
guided_practice.hint: What was Noah doing with his eyes before receiving the ball?

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the close-reading questions for The Last Pass.

exit_ticket.prompt: State one theme of The Last Pass as a complete sentence.
exit_ticket.answer: Any supported transferable theme, such as: Paying attention to the whole situation can make a person more effective than focusing only on individual skill.
exit_ticket.rubric: Complete transferable statement supported by text.

lessons.voice_prompt: Review Tuesday feedback first. Define significance and theme in plain language. Do not give the story's theme; ask Atticus what changed and what lesson that change suggests.
lessons.teacher_notes: Work showed generally solid comprehension and improved theme thinking; written precision and complete support remained the priority.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: Tuesday response work showed that Atticus often understood the text but did not always finish every required component.
lessons.course_context: The opening writing unit teaches complete evidence-based paragraphs before longer essays.
learning_objectives: Write a clear claim that answers the question.
Use two specific pieces of evidence.
Explain why each detail supports the claim.
Revise sentence boundaries and conventions.
lessons.why_it_matters: CER structure is used in English, science, history, and argument writing.

vocabulary.definition: The main answer or position you are trying to prove.
Specific information that supports the claim.
The explanation of why the evidence supports the claim.

lessons.written_instruction: Plan orally or in bullets before drafting. Use claim -> evidence -> reasoning -> evidence -> reasoning -> conclusion. Complete 7-9 sentences and use the self-check before turning the page.

worked_examples.title: Evidence vs reasoning
worked_examples.problem: Evidence: Noah starts passing more often.
worked_examples.solution: Reasoning: This shows he is using information about teammates instead of trying to dribble through every defender, which makes him more effective.
worked_examples.explanation: Reasoning tells the reader why the evidence proves the claim.

guided_practice.prompt: Say your claim aloud before writing.
Name two details you will use as evidence.

independent_practice.prompt: Write the final 7-9 sentence CER about whether Noah is a better player at the end of The Last Pass.

exit_ticket.prompt: Underline one sentence that is evidence and circle one sentence that is reasoning.
exit_ticket.rubric: Correctly distinguishes a text detail from the explanation of its significance.

lessons.voice_prompt: Model the difference between evidence and reasoning. Help Atticus plan verbally, but do not write the paragraph for him. Require the self-check at the end.
lessons.teacher_notes: Completed CER contained substantive ideas and relevant evidence. Organization, sentence boundaries, and explicit evidence-to-reasoning links remained developing.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: Tuesday introduced light interactions with materials.
lessons.course_context: The unit is building toward a model of how light travels and how material properties affect what we see.
learning_objectives: Classify observed light interactions.
Draw a directional light-path model.
Use a CER to explain which material reflected most strongly.
lessons.why_it_matters: Scientific explanations require both observations and reasoning, not labels alone.

vocabulary.definition: Light passing through a material.
Light changing direction after hitting a surface.
Light energy being taken in by a material.
Claim, Evidence, Reasoning.

lessons.written_instruction: Test mirror, white paper, foil, clear plastic, and dark material from the same distance. Record evidence, draw one light-path model, then answer the CER question with a claim, observation-based evidence, and reasoning.

worked_examples.title: CER model
worked_examples.problem: Does wax paper transmit all light?
worked_examples.solution: Claim: No. Evidence: light is visible but dimmer/blurred. Reasoning: if all light passed without interaction, the image would remain as clear and bright.
worked_examples.explanation: The reasoning links observation to the claim.

guided_practice.prompt: Before writing a claim, name one thing you actually observed.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the lab table and light-path model.
Write the CER identifying the strongest reflector.

exit_ticket.prompt: Why can you see a book even though the book does not produce visible light?
exit_ticket.answer: Light from another source reflects from the book into the eyes.

lessons.voice_prompt: Separate observation from explanation. Ask where the light starts, what it hits, and where it goes. Correct the misconception that only shiny surfaces reflect; white paper reflects diffusely.
lessons.teacher_notes: Wednesday work showed meaningful light-path reasoning; diffuse reflection and precise evidence language needed reinforcement.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: Tuesday world-map baseline identified current geographic knowledge.
lessons.course_context: This is the bridge from general map skills to Ancient Greece.
learning_objectives: Use latitude and longitude correctly.
Interpret approximate coordinates.
Explain how maps organize location information.
lessons.why_it_matters: Coordinate reasoning helps locate historical places and compare regions.

vocabulary.definition: A set of values used to identify a location.
Half of Earth, such as Northern, Southern, Eastern, or Western.

lessons.written_instruction: Review the coordinate system and complete map questions. Focus on reasoning rather than memorizing isolated places.

worked_examples.title: Coordinate reading
worked_examples.problem: A point at 30 degrees N, 20 degrees E
worked_examples.explanation: N/S comes from latitude; E/W comes from longitude.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the Wednesday latitude/longitude map activity.

exit_ticket.answer: Coordinates provide a consistent way to identify locations.

lessons.voice_prompt: Define every geography term before using it. Check whether Atticus can explain what latitude and longitude measure, not just repeat N/S and E/W.
lessons.teacher_notes: Planned map-skill bridge before Ancient Greece.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.lesson_title: Regular -ER verbs in the present tense
lessons.previous_learning: Tuesday confirmed continuing French rather than beginner placement.
lessons.course_context: The first French unit consolidates high-frequency present-tense forms before irregular verbs and broader conversation.
learning_objectives: Conjugate regular -ER verbs with common subjects.
Use complete present-tense sentences orally and in writing.
lessons.why_it_matters: Accurate verb forms are the foundation of understandable French sentences.

vocabulary.definition: The part of a verb left after removing the infinitive ending.
The letters added to the stem to match the subject.

lessons.written_instruction: For a regular -ER verb, remove -er to find the stem, then add the ending that matches the subject. Practice aloud before writing.

guided_practice.prompt: Conjugate parler for je, nous, and ils.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the Wednesday -ER verb practice and oral check.

exit_ticket.prompt: Say one sentence with nous and one with ils using regular -ER verbs.
exit_ticket.rubric: Correct subject-verb agreement and understandable pronunciation.

lessons.voice_prompt: Say each French model naturally, have Atticus repeat it, then ask him to produce a new sentence. Correct gently and let him retry.
lessons.teacher_notes: Foundation for Thursday negation with ne...pas.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.previous_learning: Tuesday introduced input, processing, storage, and output.
lessons.course_context: Algorithms and debugging come before conditionals, loops, variables, and data.
learning_objectives: Write a precise sequence of instructions.
Identify an ambiguous or incorrect step.
Revise an algorithm after testing.
lessons.why_it_matters: Programs fail when instructions are incomplete, ambiguous, or ordered incorrectly.

vocabulary.definition: A step-by-step procedure for completing a task.
Finding and fixing problems in a program or algorithm.
The order in which steps happen.

lessons.written_instruction: Write or examine step-by-step procedures, test them, identify unclear steps, and revise. Focus on precision rather than code syntax.

worked_examples.title: Ambiguous instruction
worked_examples.solution: Place the cup on the center of the marked square.

guided_practice.prompt: Find one ambiguous step in a sample algorithm and rewrite it precisely.

exit_ticket.prompt: Define debugging in your own words.
exit_ticket.answer: Finding and fixing a problem in code or instructions.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use everyday algorithms first. Make Atticus explain why a step is ambiguous and how his revision removes the ambiguity.
lessons.teacher_notes: Foundation for Thursday conditionals and online builds.

lessons.subject: pe
lessons.course_context: PE links awareness, movement quality, and coordination.
learning_objectives: Practice safe dynamic movement.
Use visual scanning before receiving or moving.
lessons.why_it_matters: Scanning and body awareness support movement decisions across sports.

vocabulary.definition: Looking around before acting to gather useful information.

lessons.written_instruction: Complete a safe movement session with scanning cues and first-touch practice.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the movement session and record one observation.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain one way scanning changed your movement decision.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use concise safety and technique cues. Do not overcomplicate the session.
lessons.teacher_notes: PE later omitted from Thursday and Friday at parent request.
